walkthroughs.title: A pause or a turn
steps: Most chart patterns fall into two groups. A continuation is a pause, and the old trend resumes after it.
A reversal forms before the trend turns the other way. Tops and bottoms live here.
Either way, a pattern isn't complete until price breaks out of it. Until then it's just a shape.

walkthroughs.title: The cup and its handle
steps: The cup is a U-shaped bowl that forms after an advance. A sharp V doesn't count.
The handle is the short pullback off the cup's right side. It should stay in the upper half of the cup.
The classic entry is a break above the top of the handle. The handle's low is a natural place for the stop.

walkthroughs.title: Lines that frame the pause
steps: A flag hangs off a sharp run, the flagpole. Its two lines run parallel and tilt against the run.
A pennant is the same idea, but its lines come together like a tiny triangle.
Triangles and wedges have converging lines too. The point where the lines meet is the apex.
In a wedge both lines slope the same way. In a triangle they don't.

questions.q: What does continuation pattern mean?
choices: A pause, then the trend resumes
A sign the trend is about to flip
Any pattern that breaks out upward
Any sideways range, whatever follows
questions.answer: A pause, then the trend resumes
questions.why: A pause, then the trend resumes. StockCharts: it forms in the middle of a trend, and the old trend resumes once it completes. Bulkowski's test is direction: price enters and leaves the pattern the same way. That works in a downtrend too, where it breaks lower. It does not make every range a continuation. Many patterns, such as a rectangle, can be either kind until price leaves.
questions.lesson_line: Continuation: in one direction, out the same direction.

wrong.A sign the trend is about to flip: That's a reversal pattern. The trend changes direction after it.
wrong.Any pattern that breaks out upward: Direction isn't the test. A continuation inside a downtrend breaks out lower.
wrong.Any sideways range, whatever follows: Not every range is one. StockCharts says many patterns, such as a rectangle, can be a reversal or a continuation. How price leaves decides it.

questions.simple: A continuation pattern is a pause, and then price keeps going the same way it was going before.

questions.q: Which word is this: a chart pattern that forms before the trend changes direction.
choices: Reversal pattern
Continuation pattern
Flag pattern
Throwback
questions.why: Reversal pattern. StockCharts: a chart pattern that forms before an existing trend reverses direction. Bulkowski's test: price enters and leaves the pattern in opposite directions. Flags and pennants are the other kind, short continuation patterns. After a continuation, the old trend resumes.
questions.lesson_line: Reversal: in one way, out the other.

wrong.Continuation pattern: A continuation is a pause. The old trend resumes after it.
wrong.Flag pattern: A flag is a continuation pattern: a short pause, then the prior move resumes.
wrong.Throwback: A throwback is a return to the breakout price after an upward breakout. It isn't a pattern.

questions.simple: A reversal pattern forms before the trend turns, so price goes in one way and comes out the other.

questions.q: What does cup with handle mean?
choices: U-shaped base plus a short pullback
Three peaks, the middle one highest
Two equal lows shaped like a W
Lower highs pressing on a flat floor
questions.answer: U-shaped base plus a short pullback
questions.why: A U-shaped base plus a short pullback. Fidelity: the cup forms after an advance and looks like a bowl or rounding bottom. StockCharts: the cup should be U-shaped, and after the high on its right side, a pullback forms the handle.
questions.lesson_line: Cup first, handle second, breakout third.

wrong.Three peaks, the middle one highest: That's three peaks. A cup is one rounded, U-shaped low.
wrong.Two equal lows shaped like a W: That's two separate lows. A cup is one rounded U, not a W.
wrong.Lower highs pressing on a flat floor: Those are straight lines closing in. A cup is a rounded bowl.

questions.simple: A cup with handle is a rounded U-shaped bowl, then a short dip on its right side before the breakout.

questions.q: On a cup with handle, what is the handle?
choices: The short pullback after the cup
The deepest low of the whole cup
The run-up before the cup began
The day price breaks out of it
questions.answer: The short pullback after the cup
questions.why: The short pullback after the cup. StockCharts: once the high forms on the cup's right side, a pullback forms the handle. It is the final pause before the breakout and usually gives back no more than a third of the cup's advance. Investopedia describes it as sloping down. It is not the cup's low, the run-up before the cup, or the breakout itself.
questions.lesson_line: The handle is the last pause before the breakout.

wrong.The deepest low of the whole cup: That's the bottom of the cup.
wrong.The run-up before the cup began: That's the prior advance. The pattern needs one, but it isn't the handle.
wrong.The day price breaks out of it: The breakout comes out of the handle. It isn't the handle.

questions.simple: The handle is the short dip after the cup's right side makes its high, the last pause before the breakout.

questions.q: A sharp V-shaped bottom is the ideal shape for the cup.
questions.why: False. StockCharts says the cup should be U-shaped like a bowl, and a V-shaped bottom is too sharp a reversal to qualify. Bulkowski and Fidelity's guide say the same. The softer U shows a real consolidation with support at its bottom. Bulkowski adds that variations are allowed, so the U need not be perfect.
questions.lesson_line: U, not V. The rounded bottom is where support gets built.
questions.simple: False, the cup should be a rounded U because a sharp V turns too fast to count.

questions.q: What does flag mean on a chart?
choices: A brief pause tilting against a run
A long base shaped like a round bowl
Two lines that meet at a point
The sharp run that comes before it
questions.answer: A brief pause tilting against a run
questions.why: A brief pause tilting against a run. StockCharts calls a flag a small rectangle that slopes against the previous trend, with price held between two parallel lines. Bulkowski adds that it hangs off a flagpole, a quick run. Converging lines would make it a pennant instead.
questions.lesson_line: A flag leans against the move it interrupts.

wrong.A long base shaped like a round bowl: That's a rounding bottom, or the cup of a cup with handle.
wrong.The sharp run that comes before it: That's the flagpole. The flag is the pause that hangs off it.
wrong.Two lines that meet at a point: Converging lines make a pennant or a triangle. A flag's lines run parallel.

questions.simple: A flag is a short pause that leans against the sharp move before it, between two parallel lines.

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: A short pause can hang off a sharp, near-straight run called the ___.
questions.why: Flagpole. StockCharts: flags and pennants must be preceded by a sharp advance or decline, and the flagpole measures that move. Bulkowski: without a straight-line or quick run, you don't have a flag.
questions.lesson_line: No pole, no flag.
questions.simple: It is the flagpole, the sharp run that the flag hangs off, and with no pole there is no flag.

questions.q: What does pennant mean?
choices: A tiny triangle after a sharp move
A long, flat-topped base of weeks
A flag-like pause with parallel lines
A deep U-shaped base with a handle
questions.answer: A tiny triangle after a sharp move
questions.why: A tiny triangle after a sharp move. StockCharts calls a pennant a small symmetrical triangle that begins wide and converges. Like a flag, it must follow a sharp advance or decline. Investopedia also describes converging lines that form a small symmetrical triangle.
questions.lesson_line: Pennant: a small triangle on a flagpole.

wrong.A long, flat-topped base of weeks: That sounds like an ascending triangle or a flat base. A pennant is short and its lines converge.
wrong.A flag-like pause with parallel lines: Parallel lines make a flag. A pennant's lines come together.

questions.simple: A pennant is a tiny triangle that forms right after a sharp move, with two lines that come together.

questions.q: A flag's two lines run parallel. A pennant's two lines come together.
questions.why: True. StockCharts: a flag's price action sits between two parallel lines, while a pennant is a small triangle whose lines converge. Bulkowski allows a flag's lines to be parallel or near parallel. Investopedia: when the lines converge, it's a wedge or pennant, not a flag. Both follow a sharp run and both are short pauses.
questions.lesson_line: Parallel lines: flag. Converging lines: pennant.
questions.simple: True, a flag's lines run side by side while a pennant's lines squeeze together toward a point.

questions.q: What does wedge mean on a chart?
choices: Narrowing lines sloping the same way
One flat line and one rising line
Parallel lines tilting against a run
A rounded low with a short dip
questions.answer: Narrowing lines sloping the same way
questions.why: Narrowing lines sloping the same way. Fidelity's guide: two trend lines, each headed in the same direction. Bulkowski: a rising wedge has two up-sloping, converging lines, and a falling wedge two down-sloping ones. That separates it from an ascending triangle, whose top line is flat. It also differs from a flag, whose lines run parallel.
questions.lesson_line: Wedge: both lines point the same way and squeeze together.

wrong.One flat line and one rising line: That's an ascending triangle. In a wedge neither line is flat.

questions.simple: A wedge has two lines that squeeze together while both slope the same way, both up or both down.

questions.q: Which word is this: a flat top line and a rising bottom line that close in on each other.
choices: Ascending triangle
Descending triangle
Symmetrical triangle
Rising wedge
questions.why: Ascending triangle. The upper line is flat and the lower line rises, so the two close in. StockCharts, Bulkowski and Fidelity's guide all draw it this way. The flat top is supply that caps price at one level. The higher lows show buyers stepping in higher, which gives it a bullish bias.
questions.lesson_line: Flat top, rising lows: ascending triangle.

wrong.Descending triangle: That's the mirror image: a flat bottom with falling highs.
wrong.Symmetrical triangle: In a symmetrical triangle neither line is flat.
wrong.Rising wedge: In a rising wedge both lines slope up.

questions.simple: It is an ascending triangle, because the top line stays flat while the lows keep rising.

reasons: stable definition; two or more publishers agree

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: A flat bottom line with lower and lower highs above it is a ___ triangle.
questions.why: Descending. The lower line is flat and the upper line falls, so the two close in. StockCharts, Bulkowski and Fidelity's guide agree on that shape. The name only says which line slopes. It does not settle the break: Fidelity's guide says most commonly downward, while Bulkowski counts upward breaks 53% of the time.
questions.lesson_line: Flat floor, falling highs: descending triangle.
questions.simple: It is a descending triangle, because the floor stays flat while each rally tops out lower.

reasons: stable definition; two or more publishers agree

questions.q: Which pattern do some chart guides also call a coil?
choices: Symmetrical triangle
Head and shoulders top
Rounding bottom
Cup with handle
questions.why: The symmetrical triangle. StockCharts, Bulkowski and Investopedia all give coil as another name for it. Its two lines converge, squeezing price toward the apex. Coil names the shape, not a result. Bulkowski says the pattern appears often but its performance is awful.
questions.lesson_line: Coil is another name for the symmetrical triangle.

wrong.Rounding bottom: That's one slow, bowl-shaped low. Nothing narrows to a point.
wrong.Head and shoulders top: Three peaks with the middle one highest. Nothing narrows to a point.
wrong.Cup with handle: A rounded cup with a handle on its right. Nothing narrows to a point.

questions.simple: The symmetrical triangle is also called a coil, because its two sloping lines squeeze price into a narrower range.

reasons: stable definition; two or more publishers agree

questions.q: On a triangle, what is the apex?
choices: Where the two lines meet
The widest part of the pattern
The breakout day's high
The first low in the pattern
questions.why: Where the two lines meet. StockCharts calls the apex the convergence of the upper and lower lines, and Bulkowski says it is where the trendlines join. Extend both lines forward to find it. It is not the breakout. Bulkowski measures a breakout as part of the way to the apex, so price usually leaves before the lines meet.
questions.lesson_line: The apex is where a triangle's lines meet.

wrong.The widest part of the pattern: The widest part is the start of the triangle, the opposite end from the apex.
wrong.The breakout day's high: The breakout is where price leaves the pattern, usually before it reaches the apex.
wrong.The first low in the pattern: That's just the first touch of the lower line.

questions.simple: The apex is the point where the triangle's two lines meet, at the narrow end of the pattern.

reasons: stable definition; two or more publishers agree

questions.q: What does double bottom mean?
choices: Two similar lows with a peak between
Two similar highs with a dip between
Three lows at about the same price
A slow, rounded low over months
questions.answer: Two similar lows with a peak between
questions.why: Two similar lows with a peak between. StockCharts describes two roughly equal troughs with a moderate peak between them. Investopedia says it looks like the letter W, with two lows at about the same level. Fidelity's guide calls it two troughs separated by a peak.
questions.lesson_line: Double bottom: a W, two lows near the same price.

wrong.Two similar highs with a dip between: Those are highs. A double bottom is built from two lows.
wrong.A slow, rounded low over months: That's a rounding bottom, one slow bowl, not two distinct lows.
wrong.Three lows at about the same price: That's a triple bottom. A double bottom has two lows.

questions.simple: A double bottom is two lows near the same price with a peak between them, so it looks like a W.

reasons: stable definition; two or more publishers agree

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: A peak, a dip, then a second peak near the same price make the shape of a ___ top.
questions.why: Double. StockCharts describes two roughly equal peaks with a moderate trough between. Schwab says the same: two peaks at about one price. Triple would need three peaks.
questions.lesson_line: Double top: two peaks near one price, with a dip between.
questions.simple: It is a double top, because two peaks at about the same price with a dip between make that shape.

reasons: stable definition; two or more publishers agree

questions.q: Which word is this: three peaks, the middle one highest, the outer two about level.
choices: Head and shoulders
Triple top
Descending triangle
Rising wedge
questions.why: Head and shoulders. The middle peak is the head, and the two lower, roughly equal peaks on either side are the shoulders. StockCharts, Bulkowski and Fidelity's guide describe it this way.
questions.lesson_line: Head above, shoulders level on either side.

wrong.Triple top: Not here. One peak, the middle one, stands above the other two. That raised peak is the head.
wrong.Rising wedge: That's two rising lines squeezing together, with no head.
wrong.Descending triangle: A triangle's lines converge to a point. Here the middle peak stands above the outer two.

questions.simple: It is a head and shoulders, because the middle peak, the head, stands above the two lower peaks beside it.

reasons: stable definition; two or more publishers agree

questions.q: In a head and shoulders top, what is the neckline?
choices: Line through the lows between peaks
Line across the two shoulder tops
The highest point of the head
The uptrend line under the whole move
questions.answer: Line through the lows between peaks
questions.why: The line through the lows between the peaks. StockCharts connects the reaction lows of each peak, and Bulkowski says it joins the armpits. Schwab draws it under the troughs just before and after the head. It need not be level: Bulkowski allows an up-sloping or a down-sloping neckline. The pattern isn't complete until price breaks below it.
questions.lesson_line: The neckline is the floor of the top. The break of it decides the pattern.

wrong.Line across the two shoulder tops: That line sits above the pattern's lows. The neckline runs through the lows.
wrong.The highest point of the head: That's the head's peak. It's used to measure the target, not to draw the neckline.
wrong.The uptrend line under the whole move: That's a trend line. The neckline is drawn through the pattern's own lows.

questions.simple: The neckline is the line through the low points between the peaks, and its break completes the pattern.

reasons: stable definition; two or more publishers agree

questions.q: What does inverse head and shoulders mean?
choices: Three lows, the middle one deepest
Three peaks, the middle one highest
Two equal lows with a peak between
Three equal lows in a row
questions.answer: Three lows, the middle one deepest
questions.why: Three lows, the middle one deepest. StockCharts describes three troughs with the middle trough deepest and the outer two shallower. Bulkowski calls it a 3-valley pattern with the middle valley below the others. Investopedia says it is often called a head and shoulders bottom. A triple bottom differs: its three lows sit at about the same price.
questions.lesson_line: Flip a head and shoulders top and you get the bottom version.
questions.simple: It is three lows with the deepest one in the middle, a head and shoulders turned upside down.

reasons: stable definition; two or more publishers agree

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: A rounding bottom is also called a ___ bottom.
questions.why: Saucer. The StockCharts glossary: a rounding bottom, also known as a saucer bottom, is a reversal pattern built over a long consolidation. Bulkowski calls its rims saucer lips. He looks for a rounded bowl shape, usually over many months.
questions.lesson_line: Rounding bottom and saucer: same slow bowl.
questions.simple: It is a saucer bottom: a long, slow, rounded low shaped like a bowl.

reasons: fixed before (checker added f148)

questions.q: What does rectangle mean on a chart?
choices: Sideways between flat top and bottom
A narrowing range that slopes upward
A U-shaped dip and slow recovery
Three peaks, the middle highest
questions.answer: Sideways between flat top and bottom
questions.why: Sideways between a flat top and a flat bottom. StockCharts says rectangles are also called trading ranges, consolidation zones or congestion areas. Bulkowski describes flat tops and flat bottoms between two parallel lines. The shape gives no direction by itself. StockCharts says a rectangle can be a reversal or a continuation, and it is incomplete until a breakout.
questions.lesson_line: Rectangle: flat ceiling, flat floor, price bouncing between.
questions.simple: A rectangle is price moving sideways between a flat top and a flat bottom, much like a trading range.

reasons: choices rewritten for variety before (2026-11-10)

questions.q: A chart pattern is confirmed as soon as its shape looks finished, before any breakout.
questions.why: False. Fidelity's guide says a pattern is not complete or activated until an actual breakout occurs. Bulkowski defines confirmation as the price where squiggles become a valid pattern, usually a break through its boundary. StockCharts says a rectangle is incomplete until a breakout. Until then it is only a shape that might become a pattern.
questions.lesson_line: No breakout, no pattern. The shape alone confirms nothing.
questions.simple: False, because a pattern only counts once price breaks out of it, and a finished look is not enough.

reasons: stable definition; two or more publishers agree

questions.story: A stock runs from $40 to $60 in two months. It then moves sideways in a tight range for three weeks. Next it breaks out above the range.
questions.q: Which label fits the sideways range?
choices: Continuation pattern
Trend reversal pattern
Too soon to name it
Throwback
questions.why: A continuation pattern. Bulkowski defines a continuation as price entering and leaving a pattern in the same direction. Here it came in rising and broke out above. StockCharts says a continuation forms in the middle of a trend, and the old trend resumes when it completes.
questions.lesson_line: Judge a pattern by how price enters and leaves it.

wrong.Trend reversal pattern: A reversal leaves in the opposite direction. This one came in rising and left rising.
wrong.Too soon to name it: It has already broken out above the range. Price came in rising and left rising, so you can name it.
wrong.Throwback: A throwback comes after an upward breakout, a return to the breakout price. This range came before the breakout.

questions.simple: It was a continuation pattern, because price came into the range going up and left it going up.

deeper.counter: Keep the same three-week range, but picture a long slide into it before the breakout above. Now price entered falling and left rising, and Bulkowski calls that a reversal. The box on the chart looks the same in both cases. The direction in and the direction out decide the name.

reasons: stable definition; two or more publishers agree

questions.q: Where a pattern forms decides its type, so one that forms after a big advance is a reversal.
questions.why: False. StockCharts: a pattern that forms after a big advance or decline is not automatically a reversal. Many patterns, such as a rectangle, can be either kind, and Investopedia says a wedge can be too. Bulkowski's test is how price leaves. The same direction it came in is a continuation. The opposite direction is a reversal.
questions.lesson_line: Where a pattern forms doesn't decide its type. How price leaves it does.
questions.simple: False, a pattern after a big run can be just a pause, and how price leaves it decides the type.

reasons: fixed before (statement reworded by the checker)

questions.q: Cup low $40. Right lip and breakout $50. Add the cup's depth to the breakout: what's the textbook target?
questions.why: $60. Measure the cup's depth from the right peak to the bottom, $50 less $40, and add it to the $50 breakout. StockCharts, Fidelity and Investopedia all use this method. Fidelity says to use it only as a guideline. It estimates the move. It is not a promise that price will get there.
questions.lesson_line: Cup target: the cup's depth added to the breakout. A guide, not a promise.
questions.simple: Add the cup's depth, $40 up to $50, to the $50 breakout to get $60. Use it only as a guideline.

reasons: computed key

questions.story: A stock builds a cup from $50 down to $35 and back up to $49. Then it pulls back to $38 over two weeks.
questions.q: Does that pullback count as a proper handle?
choices: No, it sank into the lower half
Yes, any dip after a cup counts
Yes, a deep handle shakes out more
No, a handle can only go sideways
questions.answer: No, it sank into the lower half
questions.why: No. The cup runs from a $35 low to $49 on its right side, so $38 sits in its lower half. Bulkowski says the handle forms in the upper half of the cup. Investopedia says to avoid overly deep handles for that reason. A handle may slope down, as Investopedia's own description shows. The fault here is depth, not slope.
questions.lesson_line: A handle that sinks into the bottom of the cup isn't a handle.

wrong.Yes, any dip after a cup counts: Where the dip ends matters. The handle should stay in the cup's upper half.
wrong.Yes, a deep handle shakes out more: Depth isn't a virtue here. Overly deep handles are the ones to avoid.
wrong.No, a handle can only go sideways: Handles can drift lower. The problem is how deep this one went.

questions.simple: No, because the dip fell to $38, deep in the lower half of the cup, and a handle should stay up high.

deeper.trap: Any dip after a cup looks like a handle, so it is tempting to buy its breakout. Check where the dip ended first. Here the cup climbs from $35 to $49, and the dip gives back most of that climb by reaching $38. StockCharts says a handle can retrace up to a third of the cup's advance, but usually not more. This dip took far more.

reasons: choices rewritten for variety before (2026-11-10); Investopedia unreachable for this check, Bulkowski confirmed

questions.q: On a cup with handle, where is the classic buy point?
choices: Just above the handle's high
At the lowest point of the cup
Halfway down the handle
At the first up day in the cup
questions.why: Just above the handle's high. IBD puts the entry at the handle's highest price plus 10 cents. Investopedia places a buy stop slightly above the handle's upper trend line. Fidelity uses the break through the cup's right side, and Bulkowski a close above the right cup rim. Before that break, Fidelity's guide says, no pattern is complete.
questions.lesson_line: Buy the break out of the handle, not a guess inside the pattern.

wrong.At the lowest point of the cup: That's buying a falling stock before any pattern exists.
wrong.Halfway down the handle: That's a guess inside the pattern, before it breaks out.
wrong.At the first up day in the cup: Far too early. The cup isn't finished and there's no handle yet.

questions.simple: The classic buy point is just above the handle's high, where price breaks out of the pattern.

questions.q: On a cup with handle, what is a lip?
choices: A high at the cup's top edge
The lowest point of the cup
The lowest price in the handle
The breakout day's close
questions.answer: A high at the cup's top edge
questions.why: A high at the cup's top edge. Fidelity's guide describes two lips, one at each end of the cup. Bulkowski measures his target from the right cup lip and wants the two rims near the same price, with some give. The handle forms after the right lip. The breakout comes after the handle.
questions.lesson_line: Two lips, one each side of the cup, near the same price.

wrong.The breakout day's close: That's the breakout. The lips come before it.
wrong.The lowest price in the handle: That's the handle's low. The lips are the cup's two top edges.

questions.simple: A lip is the high at the top edge of the cup, with one on each side near the same price.

reasons: fixed before (checker added f195)

questions.q: The flagpole runs from $20 to $30. The flag breaks out at $28. Add the pole's length to the breakout: what's the target?
questions.why: $38. The pole's length, $30 less $20, added to the $28 breakout. StockCharts applies the flagpole length to the breakout to estimate the move, and Investopedia sets the pennant target the same way. Bulkowski says a target is an estimate only.
questions.lesson_line: Flag target: the pole's length added to the breakout.
questions.simple: The target is $38, the pole's run from $20 to $30 added to the $28 breakout, and it is only an estimate.

reasons: computed key

questions.story: A stock jumps 25% in six sessions on heavy volume. It then drifts lower for eight days between two parallel lines. Volume shrinks.
questions.q: Which word fits the drift?
choices: Flag
Pennant
Rectangle
Double top
questions.why: Flag. The sharp, heavy-volume run is the flagpole, and the short drift between parallel lines is the flag. StockCharts calls a flag a small rectangle that slopes against the previous trend, with volume contracting as it forms. Bulkowski says flags are short, less than 3 weeks long, so eight days fits. If the lines converged, it would be a pennant.
questions.lesson_line: Pole, then a short parallel drift on light volume: that's a flag.

wrong.Pennant: A pennant's lines converge. These run parallel.
wrong.Double top: That needs two peaks near the same price. This is one run and a drift.
wrong.Rectangle: A flag is a small rectangle that slopes against the trend. This one drifts lower over eight days.

questions.simple: It is a flag, because a short drift between two parallel lines on light volume follows a sharp run.

reasons: stable definition; two or more publishers agree

questions.q: A flag that keeps drifting for four months is still called a flag.
questions.why: False. Flags are short pauses. Bulkowski says flags last less than three weeks, and longer patterns are rectangles or channels. StockCharts is looser, but once a flag is over 12 weeks old it calls it a rectangle. Four months is past both limits, so neither source still calls it a flag.
questions.lesson_line: A long flag stops being a flag. Call it what it has become.
questions.simple: False, flags are short pauses, so one that drifts for four months has turned into a rectangle.

deeper.trap: The sources do not agree on where a flag ends. Bulkowski cuts it at under three weeks. StockCharts allows up to 12 weeks before it calls the pattern a rectangle. A drift of two months is a flag to one and a rectangle to the other. That is why this question uses four months: past both limits.

reasons: fixed before (checker changed months to four months)

questions.q: Volume usually shrinks while a pennant forms.
questions.why: True. Investopedia says the initial move must be met with large volume, while the pennant should have weakening volume. Bulkowski found pennant volume trending down 86% of the time. Usually is not always: that count leaves room for pennants where volume does not fade. In StockCharts' flag example, volume expands again right after the breakout.
questions.lesson_line: Loud pole, quiet pennant: volume usually fades as it forms.
questions.simple: True, because volume is heavy on the sharp run before a pennant and then fades while the pennant forms.

reasons: rests on a study count (Bulkowski's 86%) that he updates over time

questions.q: On a rising wedge, at least how many touches across both lines do Bulkowski and Fidelity's guide want?
questions.why: 5. On a rising wedge, Bulkowski wants at least five touches: 3 on one trendline and 2 on the other. Fidelity's guide asks the same of a wedge before a breakout. With fewer touches, Bulkowski would not call it a good pattern yet.
questions.lesson_line: Count the touches: three on one line, two on the other.
questions.simple: They want at least 5 touches: three on one line and two on the other.

reasons: computed key

questions.q: What bias do textbooks give the rising wedge?
choices: Bearish, though prices are rising
Bullish, because prices are rising
Neutral until it reaches the apex
Bullish, the same as a falling wedge
questions.why: Bearish, though prices are rising. StockCharts calls the rising wedge bearish: the loss of upside momentum on each new high gives it that bias. Investopedia says it is usually bearish. The falling wedge is the bullish one.
questions.lesson_line: Rising wedge: higher prices, weaker pushes. Textbooks lean bearish.

wrong.Bullish, because prices are rising: Rising prices are the trap. The squeeze shows upside momentum fading.
wrong.Neutral until it reaches the apex: No bias is the symmetrical triangle's reading. The rising wedge carries a bearish one.
wrong.Bullish, the same as a falling wedge: That mixes up the two wedges. The falling wedge is the bullish one. StockCharts calls the rising wedge bearish.

questions.simple: Textbooks call the rising wedge bearish, because each push higher has less force even though price is rising.

reasons: fixed before (checker edited a wrong-note)

questions.q: Rising wedges break in both directions, not only down.
questions.why: True. Bulkowski says a rising wedge can break in any direction, but goes down 60% of the time. Investopedia calls it usually bearish, not always. So a large share still break up. Bulkowski counts the pattern as valid only when price closes outside one of the trendlines.
questions.lesson_line: A lean is not a forecast. Wait for a close outside one of the lines.
questions.simple: True, because a rising wedge breaks down more often than not, yet many still break up.

deeper.trap: Because most rising wedges break down, it is tempting to act before the break. Bulkowski counts downward breaks 60% of the time, so many still break up. He counts a wedge as valid only once price closes outside a trendline. Acting early is a bet on the shape, not on the break.

reasons: rests on a study count (Bulkowski's 60%) that he updates over time

questions.story: A stock slides for four months. Its lower highs and lower lows trace two down-sloping lines that converge. Each new low is only a bit lower.
questions.q: Which word fits?
choices: Falling wedge
Descending triangle
Bear flag
Symmetrical triangle
questions.why: Falling wedge. Both lines slope down and converge, as Bulkowski describes it. StockCharts says the shallower new lows show selling pressure easing. StockCharts and Investopedia both read it as bullish. Like any pattern, it counts only once price breaks out.
questions.lesson_line: Both lines falling and converging: falling wedge. Textbooks lean bullish.

wrong.Descending triangle: That needs a flat bottom line. Here the lows keep falling.
wrong.Bear flag: A bear flag tilts up, against the fall, between parallel lines. These lines slope down and converge.
wrong.Symmetrical triangle: Its lower line rises. Here both lines slope down.

questions.simple: It is a falling wedge, because both lines slope down and converge while each new low is only a bit lower.

reasons: stable definition; two or more publishers agree

questions.story: Over three months a stock makes lower highs and higher lows. The upper line slopes down, the lower line slopes up, and they're closing in.
questions.q: Which word fits?
choices: Symmetrical triangle
Ascending triangle
Rectangle
Rising wedge
questions.why: Symmetrical triangle. The upper line falls and the lower line rises, so they converge, as StockCharts, Bulkowski and Fidelity's guide describe it. An ascending or descending triangle has one flat line. A wedge has both lines sloping the same way. StockCharts gives this triangle no bullish or bearish bias, so the break sets the direction.
questions.lesson_line: Lower highs plus higher lows, closing in: symmetrical triangle.

wrong.Ascending triangle: That needs a flat top line.
wrong.Rectangle: A rectangle's lines are flat and parallel. They never meet.
wrong.Rising wedge: In a wedge both lines slope the same way.

questions.simple: It is a symmetrical triangle, because one line falls, the other rises, and neither line is flat.

reasons: stable definition; two or more publishers agree

questions.q: In a symmetrical triangle, where does the ideal breakout come?
choices: Half to three-quarters of the way in
Right at the apex of the triangle
In the first few days of the pattern
Only after price passes the apex
questions.answer: Half to three-quarters of the way in
questions.why: Half to three-quarters of the way in. StockCharts puts the ideal breakout at 1/2 to 3/4 of the pattern's time span. Measure from the start of the lower line to the apex. A break before halfway may be premature, and one too close to the apex may be insignificant. Bulkowski's table puts the breakout 74% of the way to the apex, inside that band.
questions.lesson_line: Good triangle breaks come before the apex, not at it.

wrong.In the first few days of the pattern: Too early. A break before the halfway point may be premature.
wrong.Only after price passes the apex: Past the apex the lines have met. There's no pattern left to break.
wrong.Right at the apex of the triangle: A break that close to the apex may be insignificant.

questions.simple: Halfway to three quarters of the way to the apex, because breaks too early or too near the apex mean less.

deeper.example: Measure the triangle from the first point of its lower line to the apex. A break early in that span may be premature. A break right near the apex may mean little, because the range has nearly run out. The middle zone, half to three-quarters of the way along, is where StockCharts wants the break.

reasons: cites a study figure (Bulkowski's 74%) that he updates over time

questions.q: When is a double bottom complete?
choices: When price clears the middle peak
When the second low holds a day
When the second low matches the first
When volume spikes at the second low
questions.answer: When price clears the middle peak
questions.why: When price clears the middle peak. StockCharts says breaking resistance from the highest point between the troughs completes it. Fidelity's guide says price must break out of the middle peak. Investopedia waits for a daily close above the first rebound's high. Matching lows and a bounce make the pattern possible. They do not finish it.
questions.lesson_line: A W isn't done until price clears the middle of the W.

wrong.When the second low holds a day: Holding is a start. The middle peak still has to break.
wrong.When the second low matches the first: Matching lows make it possible. They don't complete it.
wrong.When volume spikes at the second low: Volume at the low doesn't complete it. Only the break above the middle peak does.

questions.simple: A double bottom is complete only when price breaks above the peak between the two lows.

reasons: stable definition; two or more publishers agree

questions.q: First low $50.00, second low $49.00. How far below the first low is the second, in percent?
questions.why: 2%. $49.00 sits 2% under the $50.00 first low. StockCharts accepts a second low within 3% of the first. Investopedia says the lows should be within 3% to 4% of each other. Roughly equal lows are only one part of a double bottom. They do not complete it.
questions.lesson_line: Two lows within about 3% of each other still count as roughly equal.
questions.simple: The second low is 2% under the first, inside the 3% gap StockCharts allows, so the lows count as about equal.

reasons: computed key
fixed before (checker edited the lesson line)

questions.story: A stock peaks at $80, dips to $70, then rallies to $79.50 and turns down. It now sits at $72.
questions.q: Is the double top complete?
choices: Not yet, it must break below $70
Yes, the second peak failed
Yes, two peaks at about one price
No, the peaks must match exactly
questions.answer: Not yet, it must break below $70
questions.why: Not yet. StockCharts says breaking support from the lowest point between the peaks completes a double top. Fidelity's guide wants a break of the middle low. Here that low is $70 and the stock sits at $72. The peaks need not match: StockCharts calls a second peak within 3% of the first adequate.
questions.lesson_line: Don't jump the gun on a double top. Wait for the middle low to break.

wrong.Yes, the second peak failed: A failed second peak sets it up. It doesn't complete it.
wrong.Yes, two peaks at about one price: Two peaks make it possible. The break of support completes it.
wrong.No, the peaks must match exactly: Exact peaks aren't needed. A second peak within 3% of the first is close enough.

questions.simple: Not yet, because a double top is only complete when price breaks below $70, the low between the two peaks.

deeper.trap: Two peaks at almost the same price feel like a finished top, and the turn down from $79.50 feels like proof. It is not. Until $70 breaks, the slide is only a pullback inside a range. StockCharts calls avoiding jumping the gun perhaps the most important part of a double top. Wait for support to break with an expansion of volume.

reasons: stable definition; two or more publishers agree

questions.story: After a long climb, a stock makes three peaks: $48, $55, then $48.50. The dips between them both bottomed near $44. Price now sits at $45.
questions.q: What completes the head and shoulders top?
choices: A close under the $44 neckline
A new high above the $55 head
Another peak near the $48 shoulder
Nothing, three peaks complete it
questions.why: A close under the $44 neckline. The neckline joins the lows between the peaks, here both near $44. StockCharts: the pattern isn't complete, and the uptrend isn't reversed, until neckline support breaks. Bulkowski confirms it on a close below the neckline. At $45, the three peaks are only a warning.
questions.lesson_line: The neckline break is the signal. The shape alone is a warning.

wrong.Nothing, three peaks complete it: The pattern isn't complete until the neckline breaks.
wrong.A new high above the $55 head: That would put price above the head. The top completes on a break lower.
wrong.Another peak near the $48 shoulder: Both shoulders are already in place. The missing piece is the neckline break.

questions.simple: The top completes only when price closes under the $44 neckline, the line through the dips between the peaks.

reasons: fixed before (checker swapped f145 for f196)

questions.q: Head at $60, neckline at $50. Measure head to neckline and subtract that from the neckline. What's the target?
questions.why: $40. The head sits $60 less $50 above the neckline. StockCharts subtracts that distance from the neckline, and Fidelity's guide projects it down from the neckline. StockCharts adds that any price target is a rough guide and other factors count. The target only applies after the neckline breaks.
questions.lesson_line: Head-to-neckline height, projected down from the neckline. A guide, not a promise.
questions.simple: The target is $40, the gap from the $60 head to the $50 neckline taken off the neckline, as a rough guide.

deeper.trap: A measured target feels precise because it is arithmetic. Bulkowski calls the measure rule usually inaccurate, and StockCharts says any target is a rough guide. Use the $40 as a rough marker, not as a promise of where price will go.

reasons: computed key

questions.story: A stock builds a flat floor at $30 with lower highs above it. Textbooks call the pattern bearish. You have no position.
questions.q: What's the disciplined move?
choices: Wait for a close outside a line
Short now, the pattern is bearish
Buy now, the floor will hold
Wait for a bounce off $30, then buy
questions.answer: Wait for a close outside a line
questions.why: Wait for a close outside a line. StockCharts calls descending triangles bearish, and Fidelity's guide says they break most commonly downward. Bulkowski's data has them breaking upward 53% of the time. Bulkowski confirms the pattern only on a close outside a line. A bounce off the floor is not a breakout, so buying it is still a guess.
questions.lesson_line: Let the breakout pick the direction. The textbook bias doesn't.

wrong.Short now, the pattern is bearish: That's trading the bias. These can break either way, and the pattern isn't complete until support breaks.
wrong.Buy now, the floor will hold: Floors break too. Nothing is confirmed yet.
wrong.Wait for a bounce off $30, then buy: A bounce off the floor isn't a breakout. Bulkowski confirms the pattern only on a close outside a line.

questions.simple: Wait for a close outside one of the lines, because these can break either way despite the bearish label.

deeper.trap: The textbook label and the data disagree here. StockCharts calls the descending triangle bearish, yet Bulkowski counts upward breakouts 53% of the time. Shorting on the label alone is a bet on a lean the numbers do not back. The close outside a line removes the guess: it shows which way price actually went.

reasons: a statistic that changes as Bulkowski updates his tables (53% upward)

questions.story: A stock has traded between $20 and $25 for months. One day it drops to $19.40, then closes back at $20.60.
questions.q: Which word fits this move?
choices: Spring
Breakdown
Upthrust
Throwback
questions.why: Spring. Price dipped under the range's $20 floor to $19.40, then closed back inside at $20.60. The StockCharts glossary calls a break below support that soon reverses back above it a spring. The Wyckoff tutorial and the CMT Association say the same: under the low, then a close back within the range.
questions.lesson_line: A spring dips under support and closes back inside the range.

wrong.Breakdown: It did dip under $20, but it closed back inside the range. That close makes it a spring.
wrong.Upthrust: An upthrust happens at the range's top. This dipped under the floor.
wrong.Throwback: A throwback returns to the breakout price after an upward breakout. This stock never broke out upward.

questions.simple: It is a spring, because price broke under the $20 floor and then closed back inside the range.

deeper.trap: Not every dip under support is a spring. The test is the close: back inside the range, as here at $20.60. Wait for the close before you name it.

questions.q: What does shakeout mean?
choices: A sharp dip that scares holders out
A slow, steady slide over many months
A gap up on strong earnings news
A week of very tiny daily ranges
questions.answer: A sharp dip that scares holders out
questions.why: A sharp dip that scares holders out. The StockCharts glossary: many scared investors exit their positions on bad news or uncertainty. Investopedia: many investors exit at the same time, often at a loss, and shakeouts are usually sharp drops from recent highs.
questions.lesson_line: A shakeout runs scared holders out, and it's usually fast.

wrong.A gap up on strong earnings news: Holders are rewarded by that, not scared out.
wrong.A week of very tiny daily ranges: That's a quiet, tight market. A shakeout is sharp.
wrong.A slow, steady slide over many months: That's a slow bleed. Investopedia: in a shakeout, many investors exit at the same time, and the drop is usually sharp.

questions.simple: A shakeout is a sharp drop that scares many holders into selling at the same time, often at a loss.

questions.q: In Wyckoff's method, what is the cause?
choices: The range's build-up behind a move
The news that started the big selloff
The breakout day's volume spike
The trend before the range began
questions.answer: The range's build-up behind a move
questions.why: The range's build-up behind a move. In Wyckoff's law of cause and effect, the accumulation or distribution inside a trading range is the cause. The move out of the range is the effect. Wyckoff Analytics measures the cause with a point count on a Point-and-Figure chart. Pruden's CMT slides describe the same idea.
questions.lesson_line: Wyckoff: the range builds the cause; the trend that follows is the effect.

wrong.The news that started the big selloff: News can start a move, but Wyckoff's cause is built inside the trading range.
wrong.The breakout day's volume spike: That's the move leaving the range, the start of the effect.
wrong.The trend before the range began: That trend comes before the range. The cause is built inside it.

questions.simple: The cause is the build-up inside the trading range, and the move that comes out of the range is its effect.

reasons: fixed before (checker added f198)

questions.q: In Wyckoff's method, an accumulation range needs a spring.
questions.why: False. The Wyckoff tutorial says springs and terminal shakeouts are not required elements. Its Accumulation Schematic 1 shows a spring, and Schematic 2 shows a trading range without one. So a base with no spring can still be accumulation.
questions.lesson_line: No spring doesn't mean no base. It's optional.
questions.simple: False, a spring is optional, and one of the two Wyckoff buildup charts shows a range with no spring at all.

deeper.counter: Schematic 1 shows a spring, so it is easy to treat one as required. Schematic 2 shows a trading range with no spring at all. The tutorial calls springs not required elements.

reasons: one shared text: StockCharts republishes the Wyckoff Analytics tutorial

questions.q: What does flat base mean?
choices: Sideways for several weeks or more
A steep, sudden run on heavy volume
A V-shaped drop and fast recovery
A gap that does not fill for weeks
questions.answer: Sideways for several weeks or more
questions.why: Sideways for several weeks or more. Bulkowski says a flat base looks like a rectangle: price touches the same value multiple times over several weeks or months. IBD says the stock moves sideways rather than going on an uptrend or downtrend. A flat base is a pause, not a direction. The breakout decides what comes next.
questions.lesson_line: Flat base: the stock moves sideways, neither up nor down, for weeks.

wrong.A steep, sudden run on heavy volume: That's a flagpole, a quick run. A flat base goes sideways.
wrong.A V-shaped drop and fast recovery: A V is a sharp reversal. A base goes sideways.
wrong.A gap that does not fill for weeks: That describes a price gap, not weeks of sideways trading.

questions.simple: A flat base is a stock moving sideways for weeks or months, neither rising nor falling much.

reasons: choices rewritten for variety before (2026-11-10); IBD shows only its opening, Bulkowski confirmed

questions.q: What does Darvas box mean?
choices: A range set by recent highs and lows
A rounded base with a short handle
A flat top with steadily rising lows
Three peaks, with the middle highest
questions.answer: A range set by recent highs and lows
questions.why: A range set by recent highs and lows. Investopedia says it places price in a box based on recent highs and lows. The buy signal is a break above the box on strong volume. Bulkowski sets the box top at a high that holds for the next three days. Then he waits for a close outside the box. It is a range, not a shape like a cup.
questions.lesson_line: Darvas box: a top, a bottom, and a trade on the break.
questions.simple: A Darvas box is a price range framed by recent highs and lows, and the trade comes on a break above it.

reasons: choices rewritten for variety before (2026-11-10); Investopedia unreachable for this check, Bulkowski confirmed

questions.q: A pattern's measured target tells you how far price will go.
questions.why: False. The measure rule uses the pattern's height to estimate a move after the breakout. Bulkowski calls the result an estimate only, and says the computation is usually inaccurate. StockCharts says any price target should serve as a rough guide, and other factors should also be considered. A target is a reference point, not a forecast.
questions.lesson_line: A measured target is a rough guide, not a forecast.
questions.simple: False, because a measured target is only a rough guess, and price can stop short of it or run past it.

deeper.trap: A target printed on the chart looks precise, down to the cent. That precision comes from arithmetic, not from a forecast. Bulkowski says the computation varies from pattern to pattern and is usually inaccurate. StockCharts adds that other parts of technical analysis should help decide when to sell.

reasons: stable definition; two or more publishers agree

questions.q: Once a cup with handle breaks out, price rarely gives much back.

questions.lesson_line: A clean breakout still needs a stop. Nearly half gave back a lot.
questions.simple: False, many cup breakouts give back a lot, and in one study 47% dropped hard within two months.

deeper.trap: A clean breakout feels like proof. Bulkowski's numbers say otherwise: 47% of the 300 cups he studied dropped substantially within two months. A throwback to the breakout price is common too. Plan the stop before the breakout, not after the drop.

questions.story: You buy a cup with handle breakout at $50.10. The handle dipped to $47 before the breakout.

No stop until the target hits
Lower it if price gets close
Right at the $50.10 buy price

questions.q: A head and shoulders top needs an uptrend in front of it.
questions.why: True. StockCharts says that without a prior uptrend to reverse, there cannot be a head and shoulders reversal pattern. Bulkowski adds that price must have something to reverse, so a small rise into the pattern means a small expected decline. Schwab says trend reversals require strong trends leading into them.
questions.lesson_line: No uptrend before it, no head and shoulders top.
questions.simple: True, because a top is a turn down, and without an uptrend before it there is nothing to turn.

deeper.counter: Picture three peaks with the middle one highest, drawn after a long slide. The outline matches, but there is no uptrend to reverse, so StockCharts would not call it a head and shoulders top. Schwab warns that people new to technical analysis tend to see head and shoulders patterns everywhere. Check the trend leading in before you name it.

reasons: stable definition; two or more publishers agree

questions.story: After a long slide, a stock makes three lows: $30, then $26, then $30.50. The rally highs between them sit near $34.
questions.q: Which word fits?
choices: Inverse head and shoulders
Triple bottom near $30
Rounding bottom, or saucer
Head and shoulders top
questions.why: Inverse head and shoulders. The middle low, $26, is the deepest, and the outer lows at $30 and $30.50 sit near the same level. StockCharts calls this three troughs with the middle one deepest, and Bulkowski a 3-valley pattern with the middle valley below the others. A triple bottom would need three lows at about the same price.
questions.lesson_line: Deep middle low, level lows either side: the bottom version of head and shoulders.

wrong.Head and shoulders top: A top is made of peaks, not lows.
wrong.Triple bottom near $30: A triple bottom's three lows sit at about the same price. Here the middle low, $26, is far below the others.
wrong.Rounding bottom, or saucer: A saucer is one slow, rounded low over many months. Here there are three distinct lows.

questions.simple: It is an inverse head and shoulders, because the middle low at $26 is deepest and the outer lows sit near $30.

deeper.trap: A long slide and three lows close together invite the triple bottom label. Look at the depth of the middle low. A triple bottom has three lows at about the same price. Here the middle one, $26, sits well under the $30 and $30.50 lows on either side. So it is the head, not a third equal low.

reasons: stable definition; two or more publishers agree

questions.q: Which chart shows a rounding bottom best?
choices: A weekly chart
An intraday chart
A one-month daily chart
A long daily chart
questions.why: A weekly chart. StockCharts calls the rounding bottom a long-term reversal pattern best suited for weekly charts. Bulkowski says rounding bottoms are difficult to spot unless you look on the weekly scale, and the bowl usually takes many months. A short chart cuts the bowl off. Even a long daily chart is the harder place to spot it.
questions.lesson_line: Slow patterns need a zoomed-out chart. Check the weekly.

wrong.An intraday chart: Far too short. This pattern takes many months.
wrong.A one-month daily chart: A month barely covers part of the bowl.
wrong.A long daily chart: More days help, but Bulkowski says rounding bottoms are hard to spot unless you look on the weekly scale.

questions.simple: A weekly chart, because a rounding bottom takes many months and its slow curve is easiest to see there.

reasons: stable definition; two or more publishers agree

questions.q: As Investopedia uses the word, a shakeout interrupts an uptrend rather than ending it.
questions.why: True. Investopedia uses shakeout almost only for an interruption in a longer-term bullish trend. After one, it says, the previous trend often reasserts. The Wyckoff tutorial adds that shakeouts may come once an advance has started. Often is not always, so a shakeout promises no recovery.
questions.lesson_line: A shakeout is a scare, not a verdict. Often the prior trend reasserts.
questions.simple: True, a shakeout is a scare inside an uptrend, and the prior trend often comes back.

deeper.trap: Calling a drop a shakeout is no promise. Investopedia says the prior trend often reasserts, not that it must. The Wyckoff tutorial says shakeouts aim to make holders sell to large operators.

reasons: fixed before (statement rewritten by the checker)

questions.story: A stock breaks out of an ascending triangle at $40. It rises to $41.50, stalls, then closes below the triangle's low at $36.
questions.q: What does Bulkowski call this?
choices: A busted pattern
A routine throwback
A Wyckoff spring
A bullish shakeout
questions.why: A busted pattern. Bulkowski's rule: price rises less than 10% after the breakout, reverses, and closes below the bottom of the pattern. Here it went from $40 to $41.50, then closed at $36, under the triangle's low. Fidelity's guide calls this a failed breakout, or trap. A throwback only returns to the breakout price.
questions.lesson_line: When a breakout fails and price exits the other side, respect it.

wrong.A routine throwback: A throwback returns to the breakout price. This fell through the whole pattern.
wrong.A Wyckoff spring: A spring dips under support and closes back inside. This closed below the whole triangle.
wrong.A bullish shakeout: Not here. Price gained less than 10%, then closed below the whole triangle. Bulkowski calls that busted.

questions.simple: Bulkowski calls it a busted pattern, because price rose less than 10% and then closed below the whole triangle.

deeper.trap: Calling it a shakeout and waiting for a bounce is the trap. The close below the triangle's low says the breakout failed. Bulkowski adds that a busted pattern can start a trend in the new direction.

reasons: fixed before (checker added f183)

questions.story: You bought a flag breakout. Its measured target is $38. Price stalls at $36, then the whole market sells off hard.
questions.q: Do you hold on for the $38 target?
choices: No, reassess: conditions changed
Yes, the target is the plan
Yes, and add to get there faster
No, widen the stop to give it room
questions.why: No, reassess: conditions changed. Fidelity's pattern guide lists sticking with a pattern's original target after conditions change as a dangerous habit. Bulkowski calls any target an estimate only, and StockCharts a rough guide. Reassess with your stop in place. That does not mean adding to the trade or widening the stop.
questions.lesson_line: The target was an estimate made earlier. Trade what's in front of you now.

wrong.Yes, the target is the plan: A target is an estimate, not a promise from the market.
wrong.Yes, and add to get there faster: Adding into a selloff to chase a target doubles down on an estimate.
wrong.No, widen the stop to give it room: That raises the loss you planned for. Bulkowski's advice runs the other way: raise the stop as price rises.

questions.simple: No, reassess the trade, because the target was only an estimate and the market has changed since you set it.

deeper.trap: A target set before a market selloff is a guess about a market that has changed. Fidelity's guide calls holding to it a dangerous habit. The disciplined moves cut risk: keep the stop where it is, or sell. Adding or widening the stop does the opposite.

reasons: fixed before (question reworded by the checker)

questions.story: A stock forms what looks like an inverse head and shoulders. It's at $33, just under its $34 neckline. A friend wants to buy now to get in early.
questions.q: What does the textbook say?
choices: Wait for the close above $34
Buy now, the shape is done
Buy half now, half at $34
Wait for a retest of the head's low
questions.why: Wait for the close above $34. Bulkowski says to wait for confirmation before placing a trade, and he confirms this pattern on a close above the neckline. StockCharts says the neckline break must come convincingly, with an expansion of volume. Fidelity's guide says a pattern is not complete or activated until an actual breakout occurs. That is the textbook view the question asks for.
questions.lesson_line: Early is a guess. The neckline break is the signal.

wrong.Buy now, the shape is done: A shape isn't a pattern until it breaks out.
wrong.Buy half now, half at $34: Half bought on a guess is still a guess. Our rule is the full size at one price, with no adding.
wrong.Wait for a retest of the head's low: A drop back to the head's low would spoil the shape. The signal is a close above $34.

questions.simple: Wait for a close above $34, because the pattern is not confirmed until price breaks the neckline.

deeper.trap: Buying at $33 feels like a better price than the breakout. The cost is that the shape may never confirm. Schwab says many investors have paid a steep price for placing a trade without waiting for signals confirming the pattern. A slightly better fill is little help if the neckline holds and the stock turns down.

reasons: keyed as the textbook view; UCT's own entry timing on a neckline break (close or intraday) is not in the rulebook

questions.q: In Bulkowski's count, ascending triangles break down as well as up.
questions.why: True. Bulkowski counts upward breakouts 63% of the time, so the rest break down. Fidelity's guide says prices can break in either direction, but more commonly upward. StockCharts gives the pattern a bullish bias from its rising lows. A bias is a lean, not a promise. Wait for the break to show the direction.
questions.lesson_line: Bullish bias, not a guarantee. Plan for the break you don't expect.
questions.simple: True, because Bulkowski counts upward breakouts 63% of the time, so the rest break down.

deeper.trap: The flat top and rising lows look like buyers winning. So it is easy to buy early, hoping for the upside break. Bulkowski's own count still has a share of these breaking down. Let the break show the direction before you act.

reasons: rests on a study count (Bulkowski's 63%) that he updates over time

questions.q: Wedges rank among the best-performing chart patterns.
questions.why: False. Bulkowski says rising wedges, especially with downward breakouts, are some of the worst performing chart patterns. He calls the falling wedge a poor performer among bullish patterns. Fidelity's guide says performance in both types is below average, and retracements are very common.
questions.lesson_line: Wedges test poorly in Bulkowski's and Fidelity's reviews.
questions.simple: False, because tests put rising wedges among the worst patterns, and falling wedges do poorly too.

deeper.counter: Textbooks give the falling wedge a bullish bias and the rising wedge a bearish one, which can sound like a strong edge. The bias only tells you which way the break leans. Performance is a separate measure, and on Bulkowski's and Fidelity's reading both wedges rate below average.

reasons: performance rankings come from study data that is updated over time

questions.q: What separates a symmetrical triangle from a pennant?
choices: Pennants are short, after sharp runs
Pennants have two parallel lines
Triangles need a long downtrend first
Pennants come with no flagpole
questions.answer: Pennants are short, after sharp runs
questions.why: Pennants are short, after sharp runs. Investopedia: flags and pennants need a sudden shift before they form, and symmetrical triangles can form without one. StockCharts usually calls a symmetrical triangle under three weeks a pennant. Bulkowski says pennants last three weeks or less, and longer ones are symmetrical triangles. Both have converging lines.
questions.lesson_line: Same shape, different setting: a pennant hangs off a pole.

wrong.Pennants have two parallel lines: Parallel lines make a flag. A pennant's lines converge, like a triangle's.
wrong.Triangles need a long downtrend first: The trend into a symmetrical triangle can be either direction.
wrong.Pennants come with no flagpole: It's the reverse. A pennant needs a sharp move, its pole, before it.

questions.simple: A pennant is short and comes right after a sharp run, while a symmetrical triangle can form without one.

deeper.trap: Same shape, different setting. A small triangle with no sharp run before it is not a pennant, however short. A pennant that runs past three weeks becomes a symmetrical triangle in Bulkowski's book. Check the pole first, then the clock.

reasons: fixed before (checker removed absolute words from two wrong choices)

questions.q: Which word is this: three highs near one price, level lows between them, then a break below those lows.
choices: Triple top
Head and shoulders
Double top
Ascending triangle
questions.why: Triple top. StockCharts describes three equal highs followed by a break below support. Fidelity's guide describes three peaks at about the same price with two troughs between. The level lows rule out an ascending triangle, whose lower line rises.
questions.lesson_line: Triple top: three equal highs, done only when support breaks.

wrong.Head and shoulders: Its middle peak is higher than the other two.
wrong.Ascending triangle: Its lows rise toward a flat top. Here the lows are level.

questions.simple: It is a triple top, because three tries at the same high fail and then the lows between them break.

reasons: stable definition; two or more publishers agree

questions.q: Which word is this: price pokes above a range's top, then quickly closes back inside the range.
choices: Upthrust
Spring
Breakout
Throwback
questions.why: Upthrust. The Wyckoff tutorial calls it a price move above trading range resistance that quickly reverses and closes inside the range. The CMT Association describes the same sharp thrust above resistance and a quick close back below it.
questions.lesson_line: Upthrust: a push above the range that closes back inside it.

wrong.Spring: A spring dips below the range's floor, not above its top.
wrong.Breakout: Price closed back inside the range. Wyckoff names that failed push an upthrust.
wrong.Throwback: A throwback comes after an upward breakout climbs, then returns to the breakout price.

questions.simple: It is an upthrust, because price pushes above the range's top and then quickly closes back inside it.

reasons: stable definition; two or more publishers agree

Investopedia says the word is used almost only for an interruption in a longer uptrend, but the Wyckoff tutorial says shakeouts 'may also' come once an advance has started and StockCharts' glossary example is the dot-com bust, a decline. So no question says shakeouts usually come in uptrends: q46 keys the broad meaning; q57 (rewritten by the checker) keys only that a shakeout does not by itself mean the uptrend is over (Investopedia: the prior trend often reasserts; Wyckoff: shakeouts inside an advance).
